title: ctype.h: character classification and conversion; unsigned-char precondition
learningObjectives: Identify common character-classification functions in <ctype.h> and explain what each tests.
Explain the EOF-or-unsigned-char argument requirement and why a negative plain char can violate it.
Read input with int so every byte value remains distinct from EOF.
Use tolower and toupper safely and interpret their integer return values.
Describe the effects of the active C locale and the single-byte scope of ctype.
Design and test byte-oriented text processing for EOF, signed char and non-ASCII input.

understand.concept: The <ctype.h> header declares functions and macros that classify a single character value or convert its case. Examples include isalpha, isdigit, isspace, isalnum, islower, isupper, ispunct, tolower and toupper. Their argument contract is strict: the value must be EOF or representable as unsigned char. A negative value produced by converting a byte to a signed plain char is not a valid argument unless it is exactly EOF. Passing any other out-of-range negative value causes undefined behaviour.
understand.whyItMatters: Text-processing code often reads bytes whose high bit is set. On implementations where plain char is signed, those bytes may become negative. Passing such a value directly to a ctype function can trigger undefined behaviour even though the input came from a file or standard input. Correct conversion protects the program and makes byte-level assumptions explicit.
understand.analogy: Think of a ctype function as a tool that accepts either a special end-of-input marker or a byte in the range supported by unsigned char. Converting a signed byte back to unsigned char puts an ordinary byte into the tool's accepted range.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy describes only the argument range. It does not make ctype functions Unicode-aware, guarantee identical locale classifications, or define how an application should interpret arbitrary encoded text.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Classification functions

Include <ctype.h> to use the character classification and conversion interfaces. isalpha tests for a letter in the current locale; isdigit tests for a decimal digit; isalnum accepts letters or digits; isspace tests whitespace; islower and isupper test case; and ispunct tests punctuation. Other functions include isprint, isgraph, iscntrl and isxdigit.

A classification function returns zero when the condition is false and a nonzero value when it is true. Do not assume the true result must be exactly 1. Use it as a condition or normalize it explicitly when storing a Boolean-like result.

## 2. The unsigned-char rule

The argument to every ctype function must be EOF or a value representable as unsigned char. A common safe pattern for a byte already stored in char is isalpha((unsigned char)ch). The cast must happen before the call. This is especially important when plain char is signed and the stored byte has its high bit set.

Do not cast an input value to unsigned char before checking for EOF. getchar returns int precisely so it can represent every possible unsigned-char value and the distinct EOF sentinel. Read into an int, compare with EOF, and only then pass the value to a ctype function or convert it to unsigned char.

## 3. Case conversion

tolower converts an uppercase character to its lowercase counterpart when the active locale defines such a mapping; otherwise it returns the input value unchanged. toupper works in the opposite direction. Their arguments obey the same EOF-or-unsigned-char rule. A safe conversion of a stored byte is tolower((unsigned char)ch). Keep the result in int while handling input sentinels, or convert it to unsigned char when storing an ordinary converted byte.

## 4. Locale and encoding boundaries

Classification and conversion behaviour is affected by the current C locale, initially the C locale unless the program changes it. The standard ctype interfaces operate on single-byte character values; they do not decode a UTF-8 sequence into a Unicode code point. A UTF-8 character outside ASCII may occupy several bytes, and classifying each byte separately does not classify the character as a whole. For Unicode-aware text, use a deliberate decoding and Unicode library strategy rather than treating ctype as a Unicode API.

## 5. Practical design rules

Use int for values returned by getchar or fgetc until after checking EOF. If a function accepts a char, cast that value to unsigned char at the ctype call. Keep locale assumptions documented, and test ordinary ASCII, empty input, end-of-file and bytes with the high bit set. Never rely on undefined behaviour as a shortcut for classifying arbitrary input.

examples.title: Count character categories safely from standard input
examples.explanation: getchar returns int, so EOF is checked before the value is converted to unsigned char. Each classification call receives a value in the permitted range. The program also checks ferror so an input failure is not silently treated as normal end-of-file.

examples.title: Convert a byte array to lowercase safely
examples.explanation: Each stored char is converted to unsigned char before it is passed to tolower. The return value is kept in int and sent to putchar. In the initial C locale, ASCII letters become lowercase while digits, spaces and punctuation remain unchanged.

practise.guidedTask: Run Example 1 with Abc 123! followed by a newline. Predict the three counts, then run it with empty input. Explain why the loop variable is int and why the cast occurs only after the EOF check.
practise.independentTask: Write a byte-oriented text analyser that counts letters, digits, whitespace and punctuation. Read with getchar into int, handle EOF and ferror separately, and cast each non-EOF value to unsigned char before every ctype call. Add a routine that converts ASCII letters to lowercase safely. State whether your program assumes the initial C locale and whether it supports only single-byte text.
hints: The ctype argument rule is about the value passed to the function, not merely the declared type of the original variable.
Use int for getchar and fgetc results so EOF remains distinct from every possible input byte.
Check ch != EOF before converting ch to unsigned char; converting EOF first loses the sentinel distinction.
For a value stored in plain char, cast to unsigned char at the call site: isalpha((unsigned char)value).
Classification results are zero or nonzero; do not depend on a true result being exactly one.
ctype operates on single-byte values under the current C locale. It does not decode UTF-8 or provide general Unicode case folding.

questions.prompt: Which values are valid arguments to a function such as isalpha?
options: EOF or a value representable as unsigned char
Any int value, including every negative value
Only values from A through Z
questions.answer: EOF or a value representable as unsigned char
questions.explanation: The ctype contract permits EOF or a value representable as unsigned char. Other negative values are not valid arguments.

questions.prompt: Why should the result of getchar be stored in int?
options: So it can represent every input byte and the distinct EOF value
Because getchar never returns a character value
Because int automatically converts UTF-8 into Unicode
questions.answer: So it can represent every input byte and the distinct EOF value
questions.explanation: The int return type preserves all unsigned-char byte values plus the separate EOF sentinel.

questions.prompt: A byte is stored in a possibly signed plain char named value. Which call is safe?
questions.explanation: Converting to unsigned char before the call ensures the argument is in the permitted byte range.

questions.prompt: What does a true result from isdigit guarantee?
options: A nonzero result, not necessarily exactly 1
Exactly the integer 1 on every implementation
A converted digit character is returned
questions.answer: A nonzero result, not necessarily exactly 1
questions.explanation: Classification functions return zero for false and a nonzero value for true. They do not promise the exact value one.

questions.prompt: Which statement about ctype and UTF-8 is correct?
options: ctype classifies single-byte values according to the current C locale; it does not decode UTF-8 code points
Calling isalpha on each UTF-8 byte classifies the complete Unicode character
tolower performs full Unicode case folding for every language
questions.answer: ctype classifies single-byte values according to the current C locale; it does not decode UTF-8 code points
questions.explanation: The standard ctype interfaces accept EOF or unsigned-char-range values and are not Unicode decoding or full Unicode case-folding APIs.
